newsitem.title: USA: Israeli ambassador says Syria preparing for war.
newsitem.headline: Israeli ambassador says Syria preparing for war.

text.p: Israeli ambassador Eliahu Ben-Elissar accused Syria on Wednesday of preparing for war and said Israel's readiness had declined because the United States supplied advanced arms to Egypt and other Arab states.
Syria was the greatest threat to Israel in the short run, he told American defense writers at a breakfast meeting.
The Syrians have declared themselves ready for peace negotiations "but they are preparing for war," he added.
Ben-Elissar stressed that Syria's military chief of staff recently stated that "negotiations are not the only option."
The envoy also said Damascus "is trying hard to improve their (military) forces in all directions," especially in acquiring SCUD C missiles and chemical weapons.
But he said Syria behaved no differently toward Israel under the current Likud government than it had under the previous Labor government.
The longer-range threat to Israel is Iran, he said.

As for Israel's vaunted edge over other Middle East military forces, the envoy said, "When the United States says that they will do everything in order to safeguard Israel's qualitative edge, we all ought to take into consideration that this edge has diminished with time."
Inflation and the fact that U.S. aid has stood constant at $3 billion a year are one factor, he said.
But the main factor is that "Egypt and other Arab countries are getting today basically the same equipment as Israelis are getting," including F-16 fighters, he said.

Israel's defense minister is soon to visit Washington to discuss this issue with Defense Secretary William Cohen and to discuss what the United States might do to help rectify the situation, Ben-Elissar said.
The envoy refused to give details on what Israel might be seeking in terms of new weapons or other assistance.
His comment on Egypt was an unusual swipe at a country with whom Israel has a peace treaty.

Ben-Elissar also refused to defend Cairo against U.S. congressmen who sought to deny Egypt this year its specific traditional U.S. assistance of $2.1 billion because of concerns about its peace commitments and "emerging ties" with Libya.
"Who am I to judge Congress or to try to influence them? Why should I intervene in this," he said.

He reiterated Israeli criticisms that while Egypt has not violated the peace treaty the two sides signed in 1979, it has not engaged in the spirit of cooperation the treaty required, such as regular exchanges of people and officials.

Ben-Elissar said Israel has today the feeling that its "qualitative edge is ensured more by Israel itself than by the United States" because of the superiority of its pilots and not so much the Americans who are supplying the Egyptians and others with the same kind of equipment."
He also said that the size of the Israeli Defense Force has declined dramatically over the last 10 years.
He insisted that in a military confrontation with Syria, Israel would win.

But he also painted a gloomy picture: "If I were asked today whether the readiness of the state of Israel in case of war ... would seem sufficient, I would be hesitant ... to answer by total affirmative," he said.
"But I can't say we're not ready either. There's something in between. We should have spent more money for our defense," he said.

He predicted that if Syria launched a military action against Israel, "it might be less easy than expected" for the Jewish state to win and "the casualities might be a little higher than we would prefer to have."

Ben-Elissar said U.S. efforts to persuade Russia to end missile cooperation with Iran have not yet yielded results. He said he was confident that the Russian government is aware of, if not approving, this cooperation.
